title: What is Web API
description: Understand Web APIs and REST principles.

data.text: A **Web API** is a programmatic interface that allows different software systems to communicate with each other over the web using the **HTTP** protocol. It defines a set of rules — the *contract* — that clients and servers agree on so they can exchange data predictably. Most modern web, mobile, and IoT applications rely on Web APIs behind the scenes.

**REST** (Representational State Transfer) is the dominant architectural style for designing Web APIs. Introduced by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation, REST is not a standard or a protocol — it is a set of constraints that, when followed, produce scalable, maintainable, and interoperable services.

terms.definition: Application Programming Interface — a contract that lets one piece of software call another.
Representational State Transfer — an architectural style based on resources and HTTP verbs.
Any information that can be named — typically mapped to a URL like `/api/users/1`.
A specific URL + HTTP method combination that exposes an action on a resource.
JavaScript Object Notation — the most common data format exchanged by modern Web APIs.

data.title: The six guiding constraints of REST
items: **Stateless**: Each request contains all information the server needs. The server does not store client session state between requests.
**Client–Server**: UI concerns are separated from data storage concerns, letting them evolve independently.
**Resource-based**: URLs represent *nouns* (resources), not *verbs* (actions). Operations are expressed via HTTP methods.
**Uniform Interface**: A consistent way to address and manipulate resources (standard methods, standard representations).
**Cacheable**: Responses must declare themselves cacheable or non-cacheable so clients and intermediaries can optimize traffic.
**Layered System**: The client cannot tell whether it is talking directly to the server or to an intermediary such as a load balancer or cache.

data.caption: Lifecycle of a typical REST request from client to response.
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant API
    participant Database
    Client->>API: GET /api/users/42 (HTTP)
    API->>Database: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 42
    Database-->>API: User row
    API-->>Client: 200 OK + JSON { id: 42, name: "Ada" }

data.text: HTTP methods define the *intent* of a request. When you combine a method with a URL, you get an **endpoint** that maps cleanly onto **CRUD** operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) on a resource.

rows: Create a new resource from the request body.
Apply a partial update to a resource.

data.title: Idempotency
data.text: An **idempotent** method produces the same server state no matter how many times you call it. `GET`, `PUT`, and `DELETE` are idempotent; `POST` and `PATCH` are not.
HTTP status codes tell the client *what happened* — success, client error, or server error. Always pick the most accurate code instead of returning `200 OK` for everything.

cards.title: 2xx Success
cards.description: The request was received, understood, and accepted.
pros: Allow clients to branch on outcome
cons: Must pick the exact code; `200` for everything is an anti-pattern

cards.title: 4xx Client Errors
cards.description: The request was malformed or the client lacks permission.
pros: Distinguish auth vs validation vs missing resource
cons: Too many codes can confuse clients

cards.title: 5xx Server Errors
cards.description: The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.
pros: Signal 'retry later' to clients and proxies
cons: Never expose stack traces or sensitive internals in the response body

data.title: Don't leak internals
data.text: Return a sanitized message and a correlation ID — never raw exception details — when responding with a `5xx` status.

Before REST, many APIs used **RPC** (Remote Procedure Call) styles like SOAP and XML-RPC, where each URL was a *verb* (`/getUser`, `/createOrder`). REST flips this around: URLs are *nouns* and the HTTP method describes the action.

rows: SOAP needs special clients; gRPC needs HTTP/2

items.text: Why is `GET` considered safe but `POST` is not?
items.hint: One changes server state, the other does not.

data.title: Design your first resource layout
data.description: Before writing any C# code, sketch the URL layout and HTTP methods for a simple resource. This habit makes controllers much easier to design.
steps: Pick a resource for a blog (suggestion: `Post`).
List the endpoints you would need for full CRUD plus listing.
For each endpoint, write the HTTP method, URL, and a one-line purpose.
Decide which response code you would return for 'successfully created'.
data.expectedOutcome: A short table or list with at least 5 endpoints (GET list, GET one, POST, PUT, DELETE) and a `201 Created` plan for the POST endpoint.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: A Web API exposes a contract over HTTP for software systems to talk to each other.
REST is an architectural style built on resources, statelessness, and a uniform set of HTTP methods.
HTTP methods map directly to CRUD: GET → Read, POST → Create, PUT/PATCH → Update, DELETE → Delete.
Always return accurate status codes — they are part of the API contract.
Design your URLs around resources (nouns), not actions (verbs).
data.takeaway: REST APIs are the standard for web services: think in resources, speak in HTTP, and be honest with your status codes.
